The Harbor Survey
The harbor survey began in the spring, when the ice had cleared from the inner channel and the pilots could take the launch out at first light. Each morning the crew measured the depth at forty marked stations, wrote the readings in a bound log, and compared them with the charts drawn twenty years before.
By the middle of summer the pattern was plain. The channel had shifted toward the eastern breakwater, and the shoal off the old ferry landing had grown by almost a meter. The pilots had known this for years from the feel of the boats, but the survey gave them numbers they could show the port council.
The council voted in the autumn to dredge the eastern approach and to move two of the channel buoys. The survey crew stayed on through the winter to check the work, and their final log, bound in green cloth, is kept in the harbor office today.

East Summit 254 mm 171 mm 82 mm 233 mm
Readings are totals for each quarter, rounded to the nearest millimeter.

Seasonal Water Levels
The reservoir rises through the wet months and falls through the dry ones. The chart below
shows the average level at the end of each season over the last ten years.

Figure 1: average reservoir level at the end of winter, spring, summer, and autumn.
The lowest level comes at the end of summer, when demand is highest and the inflow is
smallest.

Notes on Garden Soil

Good garden soil holds water without staying wet. A handful squeezed in the palm should keep its shape for a moment and then crumble when pressed with a thumb.

Clay soil drains slowly and warms late in the spring. Working in leaf mold and coarse sand over several seasons opens it up and lets roots reach deeper.

Sandy soil drains quickly and loses its nutrients in heavy rain. Compost added each autumn gives it body and feeds the worms that keep it loose.

Most vegetables grow best in soil that is slightly acid. A simple test kit from the hardware store shows the level in a few minutes.

Lime raises the level slowly and should go on in the autumn, so the winter rain can carry it down. Sulfur lowers it, but more slowly still.

Whatever the soil, a layer of mulch keeps it cool in summer, holds moisture through dry weeks, and smothers most of the weeds before they start.

The harbor survey began in the spring, when the ice had cleared from the inner channel and the pilots could take the launch out at first light. Each morning the crew measured the depth at forty marked stations, wrote the readings in a bound log, and compared them with the charts drawn twenty years before.

By the middle of summer the pattern was plain. The channel had shifted toward the eastern breakwater, and the shoal off the old ferry landing had grown by almost a meter. The pilots had known this for years from the feel of the boats, but the survey gave them numbers they could show the port council.

The council voted in the autumn to dredge the eastern approach and to move two of the channel buoys. The survey crew stayed on through the winter to check the work, and their final log, bound in green cloth, is kept in the harbor office today.

Notes on Garden Soil

Good garden soil should be rich in organic matter and well-drained. A well-structured soil is the foundation of a healthy garden. It should be dark, crumbly, and have a good smell. Soil that is too sandy will not hold water or nutrients, while soil that is too clayey will not drain well and may become compacted. Adding compost or well-rotted manure can improve the structure and fertility of any soil type.

Most vegetables grow best in well-drained, loamy soil. A simple test to check your soil's texture is the squeeze test. Take a handful of moist soil and squeeze it in your hand. If it forms a ball that holds its shape but crumbles easily when poked, it is likely loamy. If it stays in a hard ball, it has high clay content. If it falls apart immediately, it is sandy.

Vegetables need a variety of nutrients to grow well. Nitrogen is essential for leafy growth, phosphorus is important for root and flower development, and potassium is vital for overall plant health. Adding organic matter like compost or manure can provide a steady supply of these nutrients.

Mulching is another important practice for maintaining healthy soil. A layer of mulch, such as straw, wood chips, or dried leaves, can help retain moisture, suppress weeds, and regulate soil temperature. As mulch decomposes, it also adds organic matter back into the soil.
